content.title: The Role of Public Sector In Sustainable Energy Finance

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

This lesson discusses the critical role of public sector investment in supporting renewable energy projects in developing countries. It highlights how governments and public financial institutions can leverage resources to mitigate investment risks, attract private sector involvement, and support early-stage projects. Learners will also explore how public investments align with international climate goals and drive economic growth, job creation, and energy access in underserved regions. The lesson provides examples of how effective public sector interventions can unlock the financing needed to scale up renewable energy projects.

This lesson explores the critical role of public sector investment in advancing renewable energy in developing countries. It highlights how governments and public financial institutions can reduce investment risks, mobilize private capital, and support early-stage projects. Learners will examine how public investments contribute to climate goals, promote energy access, and drive economic growth and job creation.
At the end of the lesson, a real-world case study example from Morocco will illustrate how the public sector collaboration with stakeholders can unlock the financing needed to scale renewable energy solutions.

concepts.title: fiscal policies
concepts.body: Fiscal policies are government strategies regarding taxation and spending to influence a country's economy.

concepts.title: public investment management (pim)
concepts.body: Public Investment Management (PIM) refers to the processes and practices used by governments to plan, execute, and oversee investments in public projects and services, ensuring efficient use of resources and maximizing social and economic benefits.

concepts.title: regulatory support and policy frameworks
concepts.body: Regulatory support and policy frameworks are structured guidelines and rules established by governments or organizations to promote, manage, and enforce practices related to energy use, sustainability, and environmental protection.

content.title: A: Governments Role in Investing in Sustainable Energy?

content.text:
As already mentioned in the Chapter 1 the transition to renewable energy systems requires significant capital and substantial investment across a wide range of activities, spanning from infrastructure development to research and capacity building. While private capital is an essential part of the global energy transition, the public sector plays a fundamental role in mobilizing and channeling financial resources where market mechanisms fall short.

Public sector finance not only supports direct investments, but it also fosters and facilitates enabling environments that reduce risks and encourage private sector participation and investments.

Where is the flow of resources and funding coming from?

At its core, public finance for renewable energy operates through a structured flow of resources. This flow begins with the sources of funding, which can be broadly categorized as international and national. International sources include multilateral and bilateral institutions such as the Green Climate Fund (GCF) - the world’s largest climate fund, mandated to support developing countries raise and realize their nationally determined contributions 💬️ (NDC) ambitions towards low-emissions, climate-resilient pathway.

Another important initiative is the Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP), which was announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021 and focused on large-scale, cross-border, or high-risk projects in Indonesia, India, Vietnam, South Africa and Senegal. In addition, national sources, including governments, state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and local financial institutions, address the specific needs and domestic priorities of energy transitions.

These above-mentioned funds and initiatives are managed and distributed through intermediaries, including development banks, governments, and innovative platforms. The intermediaries actors ensure that funds are directed toward priority areas, balancing short-term project needs with long-term policy objectives. The distribution is facilitated by a variety of financial instruments, ranging from direct subsidies, guarantees and concessional loans to equity stakes and fiscal policy incentives like tax breaks or accelerated depreciation.
Ultimately, public finance supports the implementation of a broad range of policy categories that are essential to advancing renewable energy, such as:

The diagram provides a detailed representation of the interconnected sources of funds, intermediaries, financial instruments, and policy measures and offers a comprehensive framework for understanding how public finance drives renewable energy transitions.

Other important factors that should also be highlighted are capacity building and technical assistance, which play important roles in working with the local financial system to create an enabling environment, develop financial strategies, and conduct market assessments, including collaboration with international climate funds to structure guarantees, subsidies, and concessional loans, as well as leveraging resources from international financial institutions and capital markets.

Ensuring that efficient resource allocation and effective implementation are two distinct key areas to maximizing impact.

Public sector investment in sustainable energy is driven by a confluence of environmental, economic, and social motivations.

Public sector investment in sustainable energy is motivated by a blend of environmental, economic, and social priorities.

At the national and subnational levels, investments are shaped by development goals such as poverty reduction, economic growth, gender equity, environmental protection, biodiversity conservation, financial stability, and good governance.

At the international level, public sector investment is largely guided by global frameworks and commitments, in particularly the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and other international climate commitments such as the phasing-out fossil fuels or decarbonization 💬️ by 2030 and beyond, which enables countries to leverage international resources, such as grants and financial instruments, to overcome key barriers and accelerate progress toward global climate commitments.
Environmental Considerations
At the heart of these investments lies the urgent need to combat climate change through the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions

Most governments around the world increasingly recognize that shifting to clean energy sources such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric power is critical for achieving our climate goals. The alignment of public sector investments with international climate goals and commitments is pivotal.

At the 2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP29) in Baku, Azerbaijan, developed nations reaffirmed their commitments to mobilize at least $300 billion annually by 2035, tripling the previous $100 billion target to assist developing countries in combating climate change. This agreement, as mentioned in the Chapter 1 is known as the "New Collective Quantified Goal on Climate Finance”, and it aims to support developing countries in transitioning to clean energy sources and enhancing resilience against climate-related disasters.

Beyond climate considerations, sustainable energy investments can also serve critical economic and strategic objectives. For fossil fuel-important countries, transitioning to domestically sourced renewable energy enhanced their energy security by reducing the dependency on imported fuels - which are often subjected to volatile prices and can be effected by geo-political tensions and conflict. In this way, clean energy not only addresses environmental concerns, but also strengthens national resilience and long-term economic stability. In later lessons we will discuss this more in details.
Economic Impacts

Investing in sustainable energy infrastructure stimulates job creation in new and emerging sectors, fostering economic growth and diversification. Public investments also catalyze private sector participation, drawing in additional resources and expertise. Social motivations, including improving public health through reduced air pollution and increasing energy access in underserved communities, further underpin the public sector's commitment to sustainable energy.
Public sector investments can have a profound impact on the growth of the renewable energy market.

By providing initial capital, facilitating research and development, and offering financial incentives such as tax credits and feed-in tariffs, the public sector reduces the risks associated with investing in new energy technologies. This, in turn, attracts private investment, driving down costs through economies of scale and technological advancements.

The establishment of clear regulatory frameworks and policies by governments further stimulates market growth. Policies that mandate clean energy usage, coupled with investments in grid infrastructure to accommodate variable renewable energy sources, ensure a stable market for sustainable energy products and services. Additionally, public sector investments in education and workforce training prepare a skilled labor force to support the expanding clean energy sector - all important factors to build an enabling environment for mobilizing capital and attracting investments.

Social Dimensions

According to the IEA's Government Energy Spending Tracker, since the onset of the global energy crisis in early 2022, governments worldwide have allocated approximately USD 900 billion to short-term consumer affordability measures (IEA, 2023). Despite recommendations to focus on households and industries with the greatest need, only 25% of the affordability measures are directed towards low-income households and the most affected industries.

The fight against energy poverty underscores the need for equitable access to affordable energy as a basic public service. Governments play a key role by using targeted social protection 💬️ systems to ensure vulnerable and marginalized groups are supported. In EMDE’s, broad subsidies often benefit wealthier households more than those in need. More targeted approaches can improve access, enhance equity, and support sustainable economic outcomes.

Government should prioritize support to vulnerable groups and energy poor households as a short-term solution. In the longer term, support should be provided to improve energy efficiency and empowering consumers to tackle the root cause of energy poverty (such as e.g. low efficiency of residential buildings)

The European Union provides two-thirds of government affordability support globally and has experienced some of the most significant rises in electricity and gas prices in 2022. Consumer support spending levels have risen in EMDEs due to governments compensating energy companies for operating losses incurred by maintaining stable prices during the energy crisis.

EMDE governments have allocated more funds towards consumer affordability measures (USD 140 billion) than clean energy investment support (USD 90 billion) since 2020.

Emergency measures were crucial in protecting consumers from energy price increases, but they also put significant strain on government finances due to a peak in fossil fuel subsidies in 2022. This may jeopardize some EMDE’s capacity to manage short-term relief while simultaneously tackling energy security and affordability by enhancing energy efficiency 💬️ and investing in clean energy.

Striking this balance is especially challenging in EMDEs because of existing financial and debt pressures, which will be discussed in later lessons. The majority of spending on affordability and clean energy is concentrated in advanced economies, which account for 93% of total government clean energy investment support and 85% of consumer affordability support (IEA, 2023).

content.title: B: The Role of Public Finance for Sustainable Energy Finance

content.text: Public Sector 'Above the Line' Financing

As mentioned, public sector financing is crucial for launching sustainable energy projects, particularly in regions where high upfront costs and market risks deter private investment. Development finance institutions (DFIs) such as the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO, formerly DFID), the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), and the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC) play a key role in mobilizing capital for clean energy in developing countries, where private sector participation is often limited (IMF, 2022).

By providing direct funding, subsidies, and financial incentives, governments can reduce project risks and lower the cost of clean energy technologies, making them more competitive with fossil fuels. In turn, these investments stimulate economic growth, generate jobs in the clean energy sector, and support the development of local industries.
Regulatory Support and Policy Frameworks

The public sector also plays a pivotal role in creating conducive regulatory environments for sustainable energy investment. This includes setting up clear, consistent policies and regulatory frameworks that encourage investment in clean energy. As mentioned earlier, policies such as renewable auctions, feed-in tariffs, tax incentives, and renewable energy targets can significantly enhance the attractiveness of sustainable energy investments.

By providing a stable and predictable investment landscape, governments can facilitate long-term planning and investment in clean energy projects. Institutional guidance plays a key role in ensuring the effective allocation and management of public funds for renewable energy. Establishing clear policies, regulatory frameworks, and institutions dedicated to renewable energy can enhance transparency, accountability, and efficiency in public investments. This includes setting up national energy agencies or funds specifically designed to finance renewable energy projects.
Facilitating the Ground for Collaboration

Collaboration mechanisms between the public and private sectors, such as public-private partnerships (PPPs) and concession models, can enhance the effectiveness of clean energy financing. Public-private partnerships can mobilize additional resources for sustainable energy projects. By sharing the financial burden and risks associated with large-scale renewable energy projects, governments can attract private sector investment, thus expanding their fiscal capacity without compromising their financial stability. Later in Chapter 5, PPPs will be explained in more details.

PPPs allow for sharing the risks and benefits of clean energy projects, making them more attractive to private investors. International cooperation, including support from multilateral development banks 💬️ and international financial institutions, is also essential in providing the necessary capital and expertise.

Moreover, governments can play a crucial role in partnering with international cooperation and development finance institutions to support sustainable energy financing, especially in low- and middle-income countries. Multilateral development banks and international financial institutions can provide both financial and technical assistance to enhance and assess the sustainability impact of projects and help countries transition to sustainable energy systems. This support is vital for countries that lack the financial resources or expertise to develop and implement sustainable energy projects on their own.

Energy Service Companies (ESCOs) and Energy Performance Contracts (EPCs) also play a crucial role in mobilizing investments in renewable energy and energy efficiency. ESCOs provide comprehensive energy solutions, including audits, retrofits, and performance-based financing, allowing businesses and public institutions to reduce energy costs without upfront capital. EPCs offer a financial model where project costs are repaid through energy savings, reducing investment risks for clients. By leveraging ESCOs and EPCs, governments and businesses can accelerate the transition to cleaner, more sustainable energy systems.
Public Investment Management

Enhancing the efficiency and efficacy of public expenditure management is another avenue through which governments can create fiscal space. By prioritizing spending, eliminating wasteful expenditures, and improving the efficiency of public services, governments can reallocate resources toward sustainable energy and climate resilience projects.

Governments play a key role in improving project bankability, managing risks and creating an environment for investments to flourish. Therefore, it is crucial for countries to establish sound Public Investment Management (PIM) policies and procedures.

Effective PIM ensures that public investments, particularly in capital-intensive sectors like renewable energy, are efficiently planned, executed, and monitored. PIM plays a vital role in prioritizing investments based on strategic importance and socio-economic benefits, thus ensuring that limited public funds are directed towards high-impact sustainable development and energy transition projects. Moreover, PIM frameworks incorporate risk assessment and management at the project planning stage, enabling governments to identify potential risks early and design mitigation strategies. This reduces the likelihood of project delays, cost overruns, and failures.

In addition, robust PIM frameworks help in identifying, preparing, and implementing investment projects that deliver value for money and align with national development goals. Countries can enhance investor interest and confidence by adopting long-term, ambitious clean energy strategies, including net zero commitments, as well as leveling the playing field through phasing out fossil-fuel consumption subsidies.

Such plans are most effective when backed by clear and stable policies and frameworks for accelerating the uptake of renewables and low-carbon fuels, improving energy efficiency, and enhancing regulatory frameworks for grid infrastructure and distributed solutions to support system integration and access goals.

Coupling these efforts with targeted public finance and remuneration mechanisms that foster competition, such as auctions, helps to stimulate investor appetite.
Enhancing Fiscal Space

Enhancing fiscal space is a critical strategy for governments, especially in the context of financing sustainable energy projects.

Governments typically use fiscal policy to promote strong and sustainable growth and reduce poverty. The role and objectives of fiscal policy gained prominence during the recent global economic crisis when governments stepped in to support financial systems, jump-start growth, create economic stimulus, and mitigate the impact of the crisis on vulnerable groups. Expanding this space is vital for supporting significant investments in clean energy and sustainability initiatives, which are essential for combating climate change and promoting economic development.

For instance, implementing or reforming tax systems to increase government revenue is a fundamental approach. This can include introducing or increasing taxes on carbon emissions making the emission more costly, luxury goods, or on wealth, which not only generate revenue but can also encourage more environmentally and socially responsible behaviors.

Similarly, redirecting subsidies from fossil fuels to clean energy sources can significantly enhance fiscal space. Fossil fuel subsidies are often substantial, draining considerable resources that could instead support sustainable energy development. The IMF estimated that globally, fossil fuel subsidies were $7 trillion in 2022, or 7.1 percent of GDP (IMF, 2023)

Phasing out these subsidies, while politically challenging, can free up significant funds for investment in sustainable energy projects and energy efficiency improvements. Reforming fossil fuel subsidies, perhaps by limiting them to households that lack the ability to pay for needed minimum energy services, is critical for redirecting financial flows toward clean energy. Subsidies for fossil fuels often dwarf investments in sustainable energy and perpetuate dependence on carbon-intensive energy usage. Phasing out these subsidies, while protecting vulnerable populations through targeted support, can free up substantial resources for investment in clean energy infrastructure and services.

In lesson 3 of this chapter fossil fuel subsidies will be explain in more detail.

content.text: Risk mitigation

Risk mitigation is a crucial function of the public sector in promoting sustainable energy investments, particularly in overcoming financial barriers that deter private sector participation.

Renewable energy projects often face significant challenges, including high upfront costs, long payback periods, and uncertain returns, which can make them less attractive to private investors. To address these issues, the public sector can employ a range of financial instruments and mechanisms to reduce perceived risks and create an enabling environment for investment.

For example, loan guarantees can offer assurances to lenders by committing the public sector to cover a portion of the loan in case of borrower default, thereby reducing the cost of capital for project developers. Similarly, insurance products, such as political risk insurance, protect investors from risks like policy changes, currency instability, or project delays, providing a more stable and predictable investment landscape. Another effective mechanism is first-loss protection, where the public sector agrees to absorb initial losses in a project, thus boosting investor confidence and attracting capital from risk-averse entities.

Stay tuned for deeper insights and expanded discussions on this risk mitigation strategies in the chapter 3.

Morocco’s energy needs far exceed its production capacity, with the country importing over 90% of its fossil fuels (World Bank, 2022). The country launched the Moroccan Solar Plan in 2009 to generate 2GW of solar power. The Noor Ouarzazate Solar Complex is the first solar power complex under this plan, with a capacity to generate 582 MW upon completion of all phases, making it the world’s largest concentrated solar power 💬️ (CSP) plant. It exemplifies Morocco's commitment to sustainable energy development. The complex is developed by the Moroccan Agency for Solar Energy (MASEN) in collaboration with international partners, including ACWA Power, which serves as the lead developer, majority owner, and operator of the complex (Global Infrastructure Hub, 2018). The Moroccan government facilitated the Noor project through a combination of concessional financing and supportive policies. International financial institutions, including the World Bank, the African Development Bank, and the European Investment Bank, provided over USD 3 billion in funding (Climate Investment funds, 2016). Additionally, the government offered subsidies to cover the difference between the power purchase agreement (PPA) tariffs and the grid price, ensuring the project’s financial viability.

In terms of technology, it integrates both CSP and photovoltaic (PV) technologies to harness solar energy 💬️ efficiently. CSP plants use mirrors or lenses to concentrate sunlight onto a receiver, converting it into heat to generate electricity. The complex’s CSP plants incorporate molten salt storage systems, allowing for electricity generation even after sunset. Molten salts are often used with concentrated solar plants to store thermal energy. The excess heat not used for electricity generation is diverted to molten salts and stored in insulated tanks, which can then be used to generate electricity after sunset.

The Noor Ouarzazate Solar Complex comprises four phases. Together, these plants contribute significantly to Morocco's renewable energy capacity.

Financial structure

The Noor Ouarzazate projects exemplify successful public-private partnerships 💬️ (PPPs) with competitive bidding for private sponsors to build, own, and operate the plants. The project’s investment has been financed through a combination of debt (~80%) and equity (~20%).

The initial phase, Noor I, is a 160 MW CSP plant. It was financed 80% through debt from the African Development Bank (AfDB), Agence Française de Développement, the European Union, the European Investment Bank, the World Bank, and KfW Bankengruppe. The 20% equity has been funded by the sponsors MASEN, ACWA Power, Aries Ingeneria y Sistemas, and TSK Electronica y Electricidad SA (Global Infrastructure hub, 2018).
The second phase, Noor II and III, is a 350MW generation capacity with an investment of USD 2 billion. MASEN secured the debt portion of the investment through loans from international financial institutions, including the African Development Bank, the European Investment Bank, the European Commission, the World Bank, and Agence Française de Développement. The project sponsors—ACWA Power, Sener Ingenería y Sistemas, MASEN—provided USD 400 million in equity (World Bank, 2022).
The final phase, Noor IV (72MW), has been financed through a combination of international loans, PPPs, and green bonds. KfW Bankengruppe, the German development bank, provided a loan of USD 64 million (KfW, 2017). The remaining funding has been secured through green bonds and equity investments from the sponsors, including ACWA Power, MASEN, and the Chint Gro[be1] up (ACWA Power, 2017).

Challenges accompanying the progress

The unprecedented scale of the project and the use of innovative technologies have not been without its share of challenges. The CSP technology, although innovative, has faced operational challenges, such as the 2024 molten salt leak at Noor III. The plant experienced a significant technical failure due to a leak in its molten salt storage tank. The failure was attributed to significant thermal and mechanical stresses. Repairing the system requires complex interventions and careful planning. To enhance reliability, a second, improved reservoir is under construction to complement the existing infrastructure. Both MASEN and ACWA Power shared responsibility for diagnosing, financing, and fixing the issue. (EJ Atlas, 2025). As of April 2025, the Noor III solar power plan has resumed electricity production, and a new storage tank with an improved design is under construction (Inspenet, April 2025).

There have also been several logistical challenges, including the acquisition of 3,000 hectares of land to establish the plants and the annual requirement of 2.5 to 3 million m3 of water per year for cooling (AfDB). The way the Moroccan government and the plan operators are dealing with these challenges provides valuable lessons learnt for other countries trying to develop their own greenfield sustainable energy projects. Some policy actions include:

MASEN funded a Social Development Plan through the Department of Rural Affairs (DAR)to provide services like improvement in drinking water facilities and mobile healthcare.
MASEN has set a 30% local content target that gives preference to local labor, materials and services (World Resources Institute, 2021).

Combining environmental impact with social impact and energy security
Prior to Noor, Morocco imported over 90% of its energy, mainly fossil fuels. This made the country vulnerable to global price volatility and supply disruptions (World Bank, 2022). [be1] Noor aimed to reduce this dependence by tapping into Morocco’s abundant solar resources and creating a more balanced and self-reliant energy mix. The complex contributes significantly to Morocco's renewable energy capacity, aligning with the country's goal to achieve 52% renewable energy by 2030 and reducing Morocco’s dependence on imported energy[be2] [po3] . This complex is estimated to supply power to 1.1 million Moroccan households (World Bank et al., 2017). The long-term vision also includes exporting solar power to Europe and neighboring countries through future interconnection projects.

Locally, the project has also stimulated economic growth through job creation and infrastructure development. This complex has actively engaged local communities by providing job training and investing in local infrastructure and services, such as education and healthcare facilities. Efforts were made to involve neighboring communities, such as Ghassate and Ouarzazate, in the project’s development, leading to strong local support. The project created thousands of jobs during construction and hundreds during operation, contributing to regional economic development (World Resources Institute, 2021).

At regional and global levels, this project has had a transformational impact on the energy system, demonstrating how research and development can be effectively localized. Noor emphasizes the importance of effective public-private partnerships, highlighting the need for balanced risk-sharing and long-term institutional commitment among partners. It serves as a model for large scalable solar energy projects in arid regions globally.

takeaways.title: Governments play a pivotal role in kick-starting sustainable energy projects by providing funding, subsidies, and risk mitigation measures. These investments reduce uncertainties, attract private sector participation, and support the development of clean energy infrastructure and technologies.

Strong commitment from governments worldwide is critical to implementing ambitious policies. It is also fostering international collaboration, and mobilizing resources needed to scale renewable energy and achieve global climate and energy goals.

Clear regulatory policies, phasing out fossil fuel subsidies, and creating fiscal space are important instruments in attracting financing for energy investments. Through targeted taxation, feed-in tariffs, fiscal space and financial incentives are necessary to align national energy goals with global climate commitments, fostering an equitable and sustainable energy transition.
